title: Adaptive Canary Scaling Protocol (working notes)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working doc for an adaptive canary scaling protocol — an operational pattern that combines small initial canaries, automated signal-driven ramping, and cost-aware backoffs. Goal: make canaries safer and faster to reach stable volume while keeping SLOs and cost guardrails intact.

Context / motivation:
- We currently do manual timed ramps for canaries (t0->t25%->t50% etc). That works but is slow and ties up ops bandwidth.
- Some regressions only surface at mid-traffic; others are transient. A signal-driven approach lets us accelerate low-risk changes and slow down for noisy signals.
- Must interoperate with Dedicated autoscaling and Hosted capacity fallbacks.

Key ideas (short):
- Start with micro-canary (0.5–1% traffic) for behavioral safety checks (errors, regressions).
- If pass, progressively increase by signal: immediate +2x traffic every measurement window if metrics stable, otherwise hold or rollback.
- Add cost-awareness: if unit-cost rises > X% during ramp, throttle the ramp and alert cost-ops.
- Use cohort selection & risk scoring to ensure slices are representative but bounded.

Who should read this:
- Product owners planning rollouts
- SRE/observability engineers implementing runbooks and automation
- Solutions/Support engineers who triage early canary issues

Signals to evaluate (primary + secondary):
Primary (auto-gate):
- Error rate (5xx + downstream failures) — relative increase vs baseline (10m/1h baseline).
- Latency p95 and p99 (absolute thresholds + relative delta).
- Inference quality regressions (passed eval prompts, QA alerts, user-initiated correctness signals).
Secondary (soft signals):
- Cost per token/unit increase > 15% over baseline
- Queue depth / request queuing ratio
- Telemetry anomalies in model output distributions (embedding drift, token distribution)

Measurement windows and statistical rules:
- Window size: 5m windows for fast ramps; 30m for larger slices.
- Minimum sample: 500 requests/window for meaningful error rate checks (fallback to longer window otherwise).
- Statistical test: two-sided proportion test (binomial) for error rate delta, with alpha=0.01 for automated rollback.
- For quality metrics (subjective), use pre-defined prompt-set evaluation on live slices every hour.

Traffic slicing & cohort selection:
- Deterministic hashing on user_id or request_id to ensure sticky routing across deployments.
- Risk-score buckets (low/medium/high) derived from historical error/latency/cost exposure.
- Canary cohort should include: 60% low-risk, 30% medium, 10% high (to catch surface skews).
- Exclude regulated customers and enterprise contracts by default unless explicit opt-in.

Ramp algorithm (working pseudo-protocol):
1) Initialize: 1% micro-canary, measure for 10m (or until min sample reached).
2) If primary signals within thresholds for 2 consecutive windows: multiply traffic by 2x (1->2->4%) every window.
3) Soft-stop: if cost delta > 15% or latency increases but errors stable -> pause and notify owner.
4) Hard-stop & rollback: if error rate increase statistically significant (alpha breach) OR p99 > SLO + X% for 2 windows -> immediate rollback and incident channel.
5) Reach target slice (e.g., 25%): convert to gradual ramp schedule or open A/B experiment depending on PRD.

Integration points and automation hooks:
- Feature flag platform: ramp control, override, manual freeze. Flagging must allow operator to pin to previous model.
- Orchestration: API to change routing weights; ensure idempotent operations and operation logs.
- Observability: a canary dashboard with real-time windows, auto-computed deltas, and recommended action.
- Incident playbook link: use the standard rollout-incident template, but add model-specific triage checklist (model binary, weights, quantization).

Cost & capacity guardrails:
- If unit cost > 20% above baseline across canary windows, action: throttle ramp to +1% per window and open cost review.
- Autoscaling interactions: prefer horizontal routing adjustments rather than immediate vertical scale-ups. If Dedicated capacity is saturated, automatically divert to hosted fallback model variant.

Rollbacks and partial fallbacks:
- Fast rollback: route 100% of canary traffic to previous stable model variant.
- Partial fallback: route only high-risk cohorts away while keeping low-risk cohorts on new variant to avoid losing incremental telemetry.
- Post-rollback: capture full trace dump (sampled) + inputs for offline evaluation.

Experimentation & A/B considerations:
- When the change is feature-complete and we need to validate product metrics, switch to A/B with blocking metrics and experiment analysis window (14d typical).
- Use the same cohort hashing to avoid contamination between canary and A/B.
- A/B should have pre-registered hypotheses and statistical analysis plan. Keep canary-derived safety checks active during early A/B phase.

Observability checklist (pre-rolling):
- Baseline locked (last 7d) and visible on dashboard.
- Availability of golden evaluation prompts loaded into live monitor job.
- Alerting policies scoped to canary-only vs global to avoid noise.
- Tracing enabled and sampling set to at least 5% for canary traffic.

Communication plan (template snippets):
- Pre-rollout notice (Slack + email to stake holders): brief summary, expected windows, rollback criteria, point of contact.
- During ramp: automated Slack updates at critical gating points (pass/fail/pause).
- Post-mortem: attach experiment logs, delta metrics, and plan for next attempt.

Playbook checklist (quick):
- [ ] PRD & hypothesis noted
- [ ] Feature flag ready (owner + emergency pin)
- [ ] Canary cohort defined and excluded lists applied
- [ ] Dashboards and eval prompts active
- [ ] Ramp automation job created and dry-run tested
- [ ] On-call + product owner notified

Open questions / decisions to make (notes):
- What is the recommended alpha for error-rate auto-rollback? 0.01 seems conservative, but increases false positives. Action: run backtest on last 6 months of rollouts (JIRA RLW-2150). (owner: Mateo).
- How aggressive should cost-throttling be for large models vs small models? We need model-size-aware thresholds. (owner: Lydia).
- Do we want per-customer SLA-aware canaries (i.e., automatic exclude for enterprise) or manual opt-in only? Needs legal/CS input. (owner: Jin).

Next steps / action items:
- Asha: schedule cross-team review with SRE/Observability (by 2024-12-10).
- Mateo: run historical simulation & produce false-positive/negative rates for alpha choices (JIRA RLW-2150) by 2024-12-17.
- Lydia: draft cost-sensitivity matrix for quantized vs FP16 vs upsampled runs by 2024-12-12.
- Jin: coordinate opt-in controls with customer-success for enterprise exclusion list.

Notes to self (informal):
- Need a stubbed API in the console so product can click "accelerate canary" which triggers +2x for next window (with guard).
- Keep this doc intentionally informal until we validate the algorithm in two experiments.

Appendix (short):
- Example ramp timeline: 1% (10m) -> 2% (5m) -> 4% (5m) -> 8% (10m) -> 16% (30m) -> 25% (1h)
- Typical thresholds: error-rate delta 0.5–1.0% absolute or 50% relative (whichever is smaller), p95 +30% relative to baseline, unit-cost +15–20%
- Quick reference: incident channel #rollouts, escalation: oncall -> PM -> Eng lead.

If you have ideas for specific metric calculations or want me to produce a mocked dashboard screenshot and the query set, ping me and I will add to this doc.
